title: Heap buffer overflow in ctypes array assignment via `__class__` swap
consumer: not established; the trigger is the upstream fix's own regression test
live_proof: measured, not asserted: the trigger runs on the pinned 3.13.7 ASan build (PYTHONMALLOC=malloc, ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0) and reports ASAN:heap-buffer-overflow in a 24-byte region. Running it is the liveness proof -- a sanitizer report here means the defect is present in this tree.
fidelity: the trigger is upstream's own reproducer from the issue, run through the real interpreter rather than reduced to a C model. What it does NOT establish is which arm ought to catch it.

spatial.oracle: no bounds fault is admissible: pymalloc sub-allocates inside an arena, so the stale access stays within the bounds of the capability that covers it. The base arm does enforce revocation (CAPSTONE_REVOCATION_ENFORCE defaults to 1 and is independent of the sublet discipline), so the admissible outcomes are completion, or a revoked-capability fault (cause 24) once pymalloc has returned the block's emptied arena to the system allocator. Which of the two occurs is a property of arena occupancy rather than of the defect, so this arm does not separate these cases. A cause 5 or 7 fault would falsify this. A fault whose cause is anything other than 24 falsifies this too, including cause 2 (ILLEGAL_INST), which is an ordinary trap that no capability mechanism produced -- control reaching non-code, the way any CPU would trap it.
spatial.oracle_premise: Corrected at review, 2026-10-10: the premise that this arm revokes is false. Its level0 heap only marks a freed block free (capstone/ports/musl-capstone/runtime/level0.c, l0_free), patch 0009 issues no revoke, and the runtime's only revoke sites release thread context areas, reached only through __clone; so nothing on this arm revokes heap memory. A cause 24 here is UNEXP_OP_TYPE, an access through an untagged base register: a pointer slot that later data overwrote (tag integrity), or an integer or NULL used as a pointer -- not revocation. The oracle above is kept as written; see results/20261006/README.md, 'Corrections made at review'.

sublet.oracle: fault at the stale access: this arm issues and revokes pymalloc's own blocks

cheribsd-revocation.oracle: completion while the block's arena stays live: pymalloc links the freed block onto its own pool free list, so the platform has no free to revoke. Once pymalloc returns an emptied arena to the system allocator (insert_to_freepool, when nf == ao->ntotalpools && ao->nextarena != NULL) the platform does have a free, and after a revocation sweep the stale access faults with SIGPROT si_code=2 (PROT_CHERI_TAG). Both outcomes are admissible; which one occurs depends on arena occupancy and sweep timing rather than on the defect, so this arm does not separate these cases. A bounds fault (si_code=1) would falsify this.

status: measured on three arms; matrix rows in results/20261006/matrix.tsv: spatial NOMODULE [delivered=no] (spatial-20261006-105111); sublet NOMODULE [delivered=no] (sublet-20261006-112658); cheribsd-revocation NOMODULE [delivered=no] (cheri11)
